summary: Discovery focused on unit economics across Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. Tidewater provided throughput and budget constraints; Redwood AE/SE mapped batching, KV caching, quantization levers and sketched example per-token math and pilot steps.
transcript:
00:00 Samantha Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we'll kick off. i'm Sam from Redwood, AE, with Raj and Maya from engineering. thanks for sharing time.
00:12 Mark Jensen: Sure, thanks. big agenda today is cost per token and how we could make this run inside our budget.
00:21 Raj Patel: Cool. maybe quick intros. i'm Raj, senior SE, i focus on runtime and batching.
00:27 Priya Kapoor: Priya here, I run ML Ops, curious about latencies and our 99p SLOs.
00:33 Lucas Romero: Lucas, infra/SRE, i'll care about VPC, private deployment and bandwidth.
00:40 Samantha Lee: Great. Priya, can you outline current usage and budget?
00:44 Priya Kapoor: Yeah so rough numbers, prod is ~120M tokens/month across chat and embeddings; peak concurrent sessions about 60. We have a mid-90s latency bar for chat replies under 800ms. Budget is around $6k-9k per month for inference depending on model.
01:05 Samantha Lee: Okay thanks. to set expectations, Redwood hosted pricing has model-tier differentials, but generally for the models you mentioned, our hosted is... um.. ballpark $X per 1k tokens for base models and higher for larger models. for dedicated you can typically see a 3-5x unit cost reduction depending on utilization because you're paying reserved GPU capacity.
01:32 Mark Jensen: Can you give an example? like per-million tokens or per-1k? we want to map to our $9k budget.
01:38 Raj Patel: Sure. real quick example, if hosted was, say, $0.02 per 1k tokens for the model family you're using, that's about $20 per million tokens. At 120M tokens that's $2,400. But heavier models or function calls add cost. With dedicated, if you commit to a capacity profile we often see effective unit cost drop to the $5-8 per million tokens range depending on batch efficiency and KV cache hit rates.
02:10 Priya Kapoor: Wait those ranges seem big. what's driving that variance?
02:15 Raj Patel: A few levers: 1) batching — increasing batch sizes or accumulating requests for a few milliseconds greatly improves GPU throughput; 2) prefix/KV caching — if a lot of your tokens are repeated conversation history we can cache KV layers and avoid recompute; 3) quantization/profiles — int8 or 4-bit quantized kernels can cut runtime compute without huge quality loss for many workloads. If you have high reuse of prompts, caching can drop token costs by 20-60% depending on pattern.
02:44 Lucas Romero: How does caching work with sensitive data? our compliance needs mean we might not be able to cache customer PII.
02:50 Maya Chen: Good question. caching is configurable per-route. you can disable for PII routes, or use encrypted cache keys and KMS so cached blobs are encrypted at rest. For Private deployments you control KMS/HSM and policies.
03:05 Mark Jensen: If we disabled caching for chat with PII but enabled for embeddings and non-PII stuff, what would realistic savings be?
03:13 Raj Patel: Example: if embeddings calls account for 40% of tokens and those are fully cacheable or dedupable, you might get a net 25-30% platform level saving. Chat caching depends on session reuse; if users re-open sessions a lot, prefix caching helps.
03:28 Samantha Lee: Also batching strategy matters for latency SLOs. we can recommend small window batching (5-20ms) to avoid noticeable latency impact while still improving throughput. with Dedicated you can also increase batch windows since you control capacity.
03:40 Priya Kapoor: What's the tradeoff on latency vs cost if we go aggressive on batching? our SLO is 800ms p99.
03:46 Raj Patel: You can usually batch micro-batches at the runtime level without adding more than ~20-50ms to tail latencies if configured correctly. the bigger risk is if you have highly spiky traffic and small spikes add queuing; that's where Autoscale and burst capacity comes in for Dedicated.
04:05 Mark Jensen: And what about on-prem/private — is cost essentially the cost of our infra plus Redwood license?
04:11 Samantha Lee: Yes — Private has a platform/seat fee plus the customer's infra. For regulated customers we do a platform license and provide the control plane optionally. Many customers do a hybrid: host non-sensitive workloads with Redwood hosted and private the PII workflows.
04:24 Lucas Romero: Are there fixed minimums for Dedicated or commitments?
04:27 Samantha Lee: Typically a monthly reserved capacity commit. minimum depends on the pool size but we can tailor. Commitments get you the best unit economics.
04:35 Priya Kapoor: Can you walk through a sample cost model with our numbers?
04:38 Raj Patel: Yeah let's do a simple model. you said 120M tokens/month. assume current model mix average cost baseline hosted $0.02 per 1k tokens => $2,400 as i said. But realistically with larger models, tool-calls, maybe $4k. If we move to Dedicated with 60% utilization and optimizations: batching improvements and 30% cache hit, your effective cost might drop to say $0.004 per 1k tokens which is like $480. Add the reserved capacity fee but overall net often falls within your $6k-9k budget if you include dedicated commit.
05:15 Mark Jensen: That math suggests dedicated is cheaper but requires commit. what are the ramp risks?
05:21 Raj Patel: Ramp risk is utilization, model choice, and prompt engineering. We recommend a 3-month pilot on Dedicated or a mixed approach: start hosted, run a benchmark with representative payload to produce estimated unit economics, then evaluate a Dedicated commit.
05:36 Priya Kapoor: For the benchmark what do you need from us?
05:39 Raj Patel: We'll need sample prompts, average session lengths, percent of long-form generation, and typical embedding dimensions. also an anonymized dataset for batching simulation.
05:48 Priya Kapoor: We can share that, yes. timeline might be next week.
05:52 Samantha Lee: Great. On security: we shared our SOC2 + encryption docs in the file link in the calendar invite but Raj can drop the security pack again.
06:00 Lucas Romero: On private deployments — throughput on our network is fine, but we need to know NVMe/GPUs requirements.
06:06 Maya Chen: We'll share recommended instance types and expected NVMe and memory per GPU; Dedicated also supports multi-instance pooling so you can size for peak vs baseline.
06:16 Mark Jensen: Let's talk about function calls and token accounting — do tool calls double-count tokens?
06:22 Raj Patel: Tool/function calling may add tokens for structured outputs; it's counted in the same token accounting. Some customers pre-serialize outputs or compress to reduce tokens. We'll review your tool patterns in the benchmark.
06:33 Priya Kapoor: What about model rollouts — if we change to a smaller quantized variant, will that affect quality?
06:37 Maya Chen: There can be slight quality delta; we do AB tests and evals tied to prompt sets. Redwood Optimize gives recommendations and alerts on regressions.
06:46 Mark Jensen: Are there example customers with similar token volumes and budgets?
06:50 Samantha Lee: Yes — small hedge funds and analytics teams in the 50-200M token range who've moved to Dedicated for a ~3-4x cost reduction. We'll share redacted case study links.
06:59 Lucas Romero: Anything on data residency/encryption keys?
07:02 Maya Chen: For Private you manage KMS/HSM; for Dedicated we integrate with your KMS or provide managed keys depending on contract. Audit logs and per-route retention policies are supported.
07:14 Priya Kapoor: Ok next steps again?
07:16 Samantha Lee: We'll send the pricing model, security pack, and run a benchmarking plan. Raj will run an initial batch sim with the sample set. follow-up in about two weeks.
07:27 Mark Jensen: Sounds good. thanks everyone.
07:30 Samantha Lee: Thanks all. End.

[Note: transcription contains typical auto-transcription artifacts, some proper nouns and acronyms may be garbled (e.g., K-V cash vs KV cache) and timestamps are approximate.]
